notes.why: Two eyes aimed up and out (39 degrees out and 33 up in the bont tick). The aperture mask could take a two-window shape; the outer parts would be invented.

Haller's organ reads radiant heat and carbon dioxide (Carr and Salgado 2019; Steullet and Guerin 1992). No phone input a web page can read stands in. The sheet recommends against painting warmth on skin colours; a body-detector spot is the closer stand-in and would be graded i.
Left unset on purpose: the plant's averaging would erase the passing shadow that ticks respond to.

rows: The Lone Star Tick and the dog ticks have one pair of eyes. The black-legged ticks have none.

In the tropical bont tick, of the Lone Star Tick’s genus, each eye has one lens and takes in a patch 43 degrees wide and 49 high, aimed 39 degrees out from straight ahead and 33 degrees up. The camera looks straight ahead, as you do.

A camel tick walks toward a dark disc on a pale background once the disc spans about 5 degrees, and toward the outline of a camel as small as a real one 18 metres away. The picture is blurred to match, and that reading is this app’s own.

The tropical bont tick is most sensitive to blue light near 480 nanometres, with a single peak. The picture is drawn in grey from the camera’s blue and green, and that rendering is this app’s invention.

The sheep tick, in the same genus as the black-legged ticks, has two rows of about twenty light-sensitive cells along its upper sides. In a laboratory, its nymphs did almost all their walking in the dark.

A questing tick grips a grass tip with its back two pairs of legs and holds the front pair out, ready to climb onto a passing host. Those front legs carry Haller’s organ, which smells and senses heat.

Lone Star Ticks steer by radiant heat through a covered pit on each front leg, and at least seven in ten adult females detected a square 10 centimetres across, heated to 40 degrees Celsius, from a metre away. An ordinary phone cannot sense that heat, so it is left out.

In the tropical bont tick, one receptor cell in that same organ responds most to changes in carbon dioxide of a hundredth of a percent around the level in open air. No phone records carbon dioxide, so it is left out.
Ticks also find hosts by body odour, moisture and vibration, and none of these reaches a camera.

rows.title: Eyes
rows.text: If you are a lone star tick, an abstract of an electron microscope study describes your eye as one lens of cuticle over 30 to 40 light-sensing nerve cells. If you belong to another Amblyomma species, you very likely have the same kind of eye, since the lone star tick does. If you belong to any other kind of tick, nobody has recorded what your eye is made of.
rows.note: R1 is an abstract, so the row gives only the lens and the 30 to 40 cells. The pore canals are left out, and the year is left out because no record states it.

rows.title: Where they look
rows.text: Picture the stretch of the world you take in at one time, from the left edge to the right edge. Nobody has measured how wide that stretch is for you.
rows.note: Left out R1 (Amblyomma variegatum, 43 degrees): its quote gives two values for Amblyomma without saying which belongs to which species, and field width travels only within a genus.

rows.title: Shapes
rows.text: If you are an American dog tick, an adult released in a field moves toward road edges, and an adult with its eyes removed does this less. Nobody has measured what shapes you can make out, and no other tick has been tested this way.
rows.note: R1 shows eyes matter for moving toward road edges but does not say what shapes a tick sees, so I left out any claim about shape or sharpness.

rows.title: Color
rows.text: Only one tick has been tested for color, the tropical bont tick, Amblyomma variegatum. In a test of which colors of light steer its movement, it had a single peak of sensitivity, in blue. Nobody has measured which colors you sense, or whether you sense more than one.
rows.note: Left out the 480 nm figure since it has no comparison job; R1 is a behavioral test, so it is not carried to other species.

rows.title: Questing
rows.text: If you are a lone star tick, you sense carbon dioxide, and the signal lasts longer when you have been kept in air low in carbon dioxide than in air high in it. If you are a blacklegged tick, the pores in your Haller's organ respond most to m-cresol and next most to p-cresol. Nobody has measured what the other ticks sense this way, so for you the rest is unknown.
rows.note: Left out R3 (castor bean tick questing time and dryness): it is about humidity, not chemical sensing. Left out the female detail in R1 because the quote does not state it.

rows.title: Heat
rows.text: If you are an adult female lone star tick, at least 7 in 10 of your kind can detect a warm plate the size of a hand from a meter away. If you are an American dog tick, a review of the work states that unfed adults with their Haller's organs present move toward infrared light. Nobody has measured whether other ticks sense heat in this way.
rows.note: Dropped the word "reports" per the voice check. Left out the 37 to 40 °C plate temperature and any organ-removal result, since R2's quote only states the result with organs present.

rows.title: Breath
rows.text: If you are a lone star tick, your sensing cells respond electrically to carbon dioxide, a gas animals breathe out. If you are a blacklegged tick, the sensors in your Haller's organ respond most strongly to a chemical called m-cresol, and next most to p-cresol. Nobody has measured which chemicals you sense if you are any other kind of tick.
rows.note: Left out R3 (castor bean tick questing time and dryness) because it does not state a chemical sense; did not say where cresols come from since no record states it.

rows.title: Smell, damp and footsteps
rows.text: If you are a blacklegged tick, the sensing organs in your Haller's organ respond most to m-cresol and next to p-cresol, and if you are a lone star tick, your cells respond to carbon dioxide for longer after you have been in air low in it. If you are a castor bean tick, you spend less time questing as the air dries. Nobody has measured whether you sense vibration, such as footsteps, and for most ticks nobody has measured smell either.
rows.note: No record covers vibration in any tick, so the row says it is unmeasured. R1 and R3 are abstracts, so I gave only what they state.
